vignette:
The Weight of What He Saw

Rajan is a fifty-three-year-old South Asian man who has been married to his wife, Priya, for nearly twenty-six years. He works as a painter - interiors mostly, the careful, methodical kind of work that requires patience and a steady hand. He is soft-spoken and deliberate in conversation, choosing his words the way he chooses his brushes, with intention. It takes him several sessions before he begins to speak about what happened in Colombo in the late 1990s, when he was still a young man visiting his mother's extended family during what everyone assumed would be a brief, uneventful trip home.

He was thirty-one years old when a bomb detonated in a crowded marketplace two streets from where he was standing. He remembers the sound before anything else - not the explosion itself, he says, but the silence that came immediately after, a silence so complete it felt like the world had simply stopped breathing. Then the screaming began. He ran toward the smoke because someone nearby was calling for help, and what he found there - the bodies, the blood on the white walls of a shop front, a child's sandal in the middle of the road - is something he has never fully described to anyone, including Priya.

He returned to his adopted country within two weeks, went back to his work, and told himself he had survived. For years, that was mostly true. He was busy. The children came. He built a small business. He painted walls and ceilings and trim work and let the rhythm of it carry him forward.

But the forgetting was never complete. He learned early on that the smell of certain solvents - something sharp and chemical - could send him back to that street in an instant, his heart hammering, his hands going cold. He stopped using particular brands of primer without fully understanding why. He began scheduling his work so that he was never alone in an enclosed space for too long. He told himself these were practical choices.

Over time, the nights became harder. He sleeps lightly and poorly, waking at small sounds - a car door, a neighbor's dog - with a jolt of alertness that takes long minutes to subside. He rarely speaks about his dreams, but Priya has told him that he sometimes calls out, and that in the morning he looks like a man who has been running.

He is not, by his own description, a man who falls apart. He goes to work. He eats dinner with his family. He attends temple. But there is a narrowness to his life that has grown more pronounced over the years, a careful management of where he goes and when, a reluctance to be in crowds, a particular aversion to the news when it covers bombings or war. His eldest son once asked why he always sat facing the door in restaurants, and Rajan laughed and said it was just habit.

What brings him to therapy now, more than two decades later, is something his son said - not the question about the door, but a quieter moment when the young man told him that he seemed far away sometimes, even when he was right there in the room. It landed in a way Rajan had not expected. He sat with it for several months before making an appointment.

He describes his current distress as manageable but persistent - a low hum beneath ordinary life. He says he does not feel broken, exactly. He feels like a wall that has been painted over many times, each coat holding, but the cracks underneath still there, still moving slowly toward the surface. He is not sure, he admits, that he ever really let himself understand what he saw that day. He thought, for a long time, that not understanding it was the same as being fine.
